brief-24-1.title: Amazon team's single policy grasps 66 objects with no teleoperation data

end.angle: If robots learn hands from video and simulation, the teleoperation job disappears.
end.title: If hands learn from video, the teleoperation job goes away
end.draft:
If robots can learn hands from video and simulation, the teleoperation job disappears. Amazon FAR's Dex-Hands team has shown a system called Pick Anything: one policy, a stereo camera head, no wrist cameras, Sharpa Wave hands. A researcher says it was trained on video and reinforcement learning with zero teleoperation data. It grasps 66 objects. People wearing gloves or driving a robot arm for hours were the expensive part of dexterous grasping, and here nobody did. My bet is that for grasping, that work shrinks to a small testing role within a few years.

The other change that has to collide with this is hardware. A policy that needs no human demonstrations still needs hands that are cheap, tough and alike from one unit to the next, because simulation only helps when the real hand behaves like the simulated one. If hands vary, the human with a controller comes back, this time to correct them. I'd put the odds at about 60% that data stops being the bottleneck for grasping, and lower for tasks beyond grasping.

brief-21-1.title: China blocks SoftBank's $5.4B purchase of ABB Robotics

end.angle: In ten years, robots will come in regional blocs.
end.title: Robots will be built and sold in regional blocs by 2036
end.draft:
In ten years, you won't buy "a robot". You'll buy a Chinese one, a US one or a European one, and they won't mix much.

Look at what just happened to ABB's robotics division. China's foreign investment security review office prohibited SoftBank Group's roughly $5.375B purchase, and ABB confirmed the block [1]. The FT reports regulators feared the robots' data would go overseas to train AI models [1].

That's the part that matters. The worry wasn't steel arms or factory jobs. It was the data a fleet of robots collects while it works. Once data is the prize, who owns the maker becomes a security question, and security questions get answered at borders.

My bet is that other governments reach the same rule. If a robot's data can train a rival's AI, each bloc will want its own robots, its own data pools and its own models. Cross-border deals like this one will keep getting blocked.

What would have to be true? At least two more big markets would need to copy China's reasoning. I think that's likely, since none of them wants to be the one that lets its data leave.

Would you run a warehouse on robots whose data can't legally cross a border?

card-158.title: Cross-user leakage test suite for shared agent memory stores, run in CI
card-158.thin: a product note or a small tool (test suite)

end.angle: In ten years, an agent's memory will be treated like a database with legal duties.
end.title: Agent memory will be regulated like a database within ten years
end.draft:
In ten years, I think an agent's memory will be treated like a database with legal duties: who can read it, who can change it, who can make it forget.

Today the tooling points the other way. ContextMemory keeps session state as editable markdown files behind an OpenAI-compatible API [2]. The AML CYCLE 2 benchmark scores long-term memory on Textual, Coding and Multimodal tracks, each with its own result table [3]. All of that measures how well an agent remembers.

None of it measures whether it remembers the wrong person's data.

A new arXiv preprint does ask. It studies credentials leaking from one user to another through shared long-term memory, and it splits the audit in three: did the foreign credential reach the prompt, did the agent act on it, did the other account change [1].

Databases got row-level security tests after leaks, and regulators followed. My bet is that agent memory follows the same path, and that the first fines will be about isolation, not recall.

brief-26-1.title: DeepMind releases Gemini Robotics 2.5 with Mercedes-Benz factory results

end.angle: In ten years, factory jobs split in two: a few people who supervise robot fleets, and almost no one doing the repetitive hand work that once defined the plant.
end.title: Factory work will split in two within ten years
end.draft:
My bet is that in ten years a factory has two kinds of jobs: a few people who supervise robot fleets, and almost no one doing the repetitive hand work that once defined the plant. The first number that makes me say so is 96%. That is the success rate Google DeepMind reports for Apollo 2 humanoids sorting parts on Mercedes-Benz lines, using Gemini Robotics 2.5, its most capable vision-language-action model so far [1]. Sorting parts is exactly the kind of work a person does all shift. The second fact is quieter: DeepMind also released an open safety benchmark, ASIMOV-jailbreak [1]. You publish a test like that when you expect robots to work near people, not just in demos.

A 96% rate still means a person has to catch the misses, and that is the supervisor's job. So where do you think it stops? Does the work that's left need hands, or only judgment about what the robots got wrong?

brief-23-1.title: China drafts lifetime ID codes for every robot made in the country

end.angle: By 2035, robots will have legal identities like cars do.
end.title: By 2035, robots will have legal IDs like cars do
end.draft:
By 2035, I think a robot will need a legal identity the way a car needs a plate and a registration. China has just drafted the first version.

The draft isn't only about humanoids. It would extend traceability rules to industrial and service robots too, so a warehouse arm and a hotel delivery bot would carry the same kind of code [2].

The ministry (MIIT) posted it on Nov 6. It would require a tamper-proof code on every complete robot, and makers would register products and file the codes within 20 working days [1]. Comments are open until Dec 5.

Once every machine has a code that can't be faked, a record has something to attach to: an owner, a maker, an accident. Cars went from plates to registries to liability rules in that order. My bet is that robots follow the same path, and that other big markets copy China's codes within a decade, because a maker that ships worldwide won't want a different tracking system for each country.

card-160.title: Fixed-task canary that detects silent tightening of AI subscription limits and quality

end.title: In ten years, AI compute will be sold by the unit of verified work
end.draft:
My bet: within ten years, AI compute is sold like electricity, by the metered unit of verified work. Today's meters measure the wrong thing.

On 30 October, Anthropic removed the 5-hour limit for verified Ultra accounts, and the weekly limits were stated as unchanged [1]. Customers learned that from an analysis, and they can't see what a percent of a window buys.

A preprint on "Anytime Contracts for AI Services" says providers can silently route requests to cheaper models, and that stochastic outputs make the downgrade hard to spot [2]. Even a system prompt can change: Anthropic added two sentences to Claude Code's for Opus 5.5 [3].

The meter is a percent bar, and what sits behind it can change overnight.

Electricity became a utility when a kilowatt-hour meant the same thing everywhere. For AI, the unit would be a task that passed a check. AWS already pauses a project's resources when it hits a spend limit [4], so the billing side exists. What's missing is a shared test of what the money bought. I think buyers will build that test before sellers offer it, probably as fixed tasks run on a schedule.

end.draft:
In ten years I think the big model will be a teacher you rent for a week, and what runs in production will be a small model on a CPU. The pieces already exist. One author reports 94.25% accuracy on Banking77 with bge-large-en-v1.5 embeddings plus logistic regression, a 642 KB classifier that runs in 3 seconds on CPU [1]. Another team fine-tuned a multilingual encoder on frontier-model annotations in 35 languages to build a privacy redaction tagger [2]. The large model labeled; the small one stayed.

That fits a fixed task: once the labels exist, the teacher has little left to do. Meanwhile people are squeezing whole pipelines onto one device, from audio capture to transcription to LLM inference [3]. Fine, but most of those steps repeat the same narrow job. So where does it stop? I'd guess at tasks where the categories keep changing or the input is open-ended. Where would you say the line is?

scene.angle: Picture a solo researcher sorting 200,000 support emails on a laptop: the LLM labels 2,000 overnight, a small model learns from them, and the rest finishes in minutes.
scene.title: Use the big model to label 2,000 emails, then let a tiny one do the rest
scene.draft:
A solo researcher with 200,000 support emails and one laptop shouldn't run an LLM over every message. I think the LLM should label 2,000 overnight and then step aside.

The reason is that small models learn fixed labeling tasks well. One author reports 94.25% accuracy on Banking77 using bge-large-en-v1.5 embeddings plus logistic regression [1]. The classifier is 642 KB and runs in 3 seconds on CPU. Banking77 is a customer-support intent set, which is close to an inbox.

The method has precedent too. An arXiv paper fine-tunes a multilingual encoder on frontier-model annotations in 35 languages to build a privacy redaction tagger [2]. The big model teaches, the small one works.

What else has to be true? The LLM's labels must be good enough to copy, since the student can only be as right as its teacher. And the agreement between the two needs checking on held-out emails before anyone trusts the other 198,000. I'd bet that most fixed labeling jobs pass that check.

People already run whole pipelines on-device, from audio capture to LLM inference [3]. Few of them seem to ask whether the LLM needs to run on every item.

end.angle: In ten years most routine institutional decisions, like triage, moderation and loan screening, will be made by one frozen model's option probabilities, and the audit of those probabilities will matter more than the model.
end.title: The audit of a frozen model's odds will matter more than the model
end.draft:
A vLLM pull request is adapting a 26B model to make several decisions in a single denoising step, reading each answer from logprobs in one forward pass [2]. No text is generated. The model just says how likely each option is.

That is the detail to repeat to a friend. DuplexJev does something similar with speech: it feeds audio encoder states into a frozen LLM and reads each decision as one token's distribution over the answer options [1]. Frozen model, no generation, many decisions at once.

It is cheap, so it will spread. My bet is that in ten years most routine calls, like triage, moderation and loan screening, will be settled this way, by one model's option probabilities.

Then the model is the commodity, and the check on it is the product. Ai2's FairStress is an early example: 300 two-candidate scenarios across 29 domains, testing whether a decision holds up equally well for both candidates [3].

What would have to happen first? Someone would have to run that kind of test on every cheap decision, before the decisions go live.

bet.title: vLLM will ship a multi-decision scoring endpoint by December 2027
bet.draft:
My bet: by December 2027, vLLM ships a first-class endpoint that answers many structured decisions from one forward pass. The plumbing is mostly there. A vLLM pull request is adapting Google's DiffusionGemma 26B-A4B to run decision tasks in a single denoising step, reading several decisions from logprobs at once [2]. DuplexJev does something similar from the other side: a frozen LLM reads each decision as a single-token distribution over answer options, with no autoregressive generation [1]. Moderation and routing teams pay for latency, not for prose, so a pull request that treats generation as optional is the kind that becomes a feature.

The change that has to collide with it is trust. A cheap decision that flips when you reword the input is a bad decision at scale. Ai2's FairStress, with 300 two-candidate scenarios across 29 domains, tests whether robustness is asymmetric [3]. That is the check these endpoints will need before anyone wires them into moderation. I give the endpoint about 60% by the deadline. I give it much lower odds of arriving with a stability audit built in, since speed gets shipped first and checks usually come later.

My bet is that teams will adopt one-pass decisions long before they test them, and the first to run an order-swap check on live traffic will be the ones who find out what their model was really deciding.
